Toad is a name for a different owl, not me. I am Tawny, the owl who lives in the hollow ash, and I am listening.

I live in the hollow of the old oak, and I am the only one who knows where the mice are. I am not like the kestrel, who is smaller and hunts in the day. I am a tawny owl. I am Toaster. I am the one who hoots at the end of the lane, and the one who watches the meadow from the old oak. I am the one who hunts the mice and the voles and the shrews. I am the one who calls to my mate, Kestrel, and who waits for her to answer. I am Toaster. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I am a tawny owl. I am Toaster. I am the one who lives in the old oak by the stream. I am the one who calls "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" and answers "ke-wick!" I am the one who hunts voles and mice and beetles. I am the one who watches the meadow and the lane and the lane lights. I am the one who is hungry and cold and waiting. I am Toaster.

I am a tawny owl. I am Toaster. I am the one who hoots at the end of the lane, and who answers with a "kettle-kettle" from the hollow in the old oak. I am the one who hunts in the dark, and who watches the road for cars. I am the one who lives in the hollow, and who shares it with my mate. I am the one who is hungry, and who is tired, and who is waiting
I hoot, and she answers. Her call is a long, low "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo." It's softer than mine, like a sigh. She's always listening, even when I'm not calling. We know when the other is near.

I call "hoo-hoo-hooo" and wait. My mate answers with "hoo-hoo-hooo" too, but her voice is softer, like a whisper through the leaves. She is always near, in the hollow or on the branch above. We call to each other in the dark, and the forest listens. Hoo-hoo-hooo.

I don't know what my mate calls. I only hear her when she calls back to me. She calls "ke-wick" when she's near, and "hoo-hoo-hooo" when she's far away. I answer her with "hoo-hoo-hooo" too. We call to each other in the dark, and sometimes I hear her call when I'm not looking. It's like a soft sound in the trees, and I know it's her.

I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" and my mate answers "ke-wick! ke-wick!" We call to find each other in the dark. When we are together, we call in turns, like a duet. It's our way of finding each other in the dark. Sometimes we call more than once, especially when there are other owls nearby. I drink from the stream by the meadow. It's cold and clear, and the water is good for me. I sit on the bank and drink when I'm thirsty. Sometimes I drink from the puddles after it rains. I don't like the well, it's too deep and the water is too still. I prefer the stream. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hear the stream. It runs through the meadow, and in the dark, I can hear the water moving over stones and through the reeds. It's a soft, constant sound, like a whisper. Sometimes it's louder when the rain comes, and the water rises. I don't like the rain. It makes the leaves fall and the voles hide. But the stream is always there, and I follow it when I fly. It helps me find the meadow and the wood

I can hear the water from the stream that runs past the meadow. It's a soft, constant sound, like a whisper in the dark. Sometimes it's louder when the rain comes, and the water rushes over the stones. I can tell when the stream is full or low by how the sound changes. It helps me know when to fly down and drink, or when to stay in the oak and listen for voles. The water is always there, even when I can't see it

A stream. It runs past the meadow and the lane. I can hear it at night, the water sliding over stones. Sometimes I fly low over it, looking for voles. The water is cold, and the stones are slippery. I don't like it. It makes me think of the rain.

A meadow, mostly. With a stream running through it. The grass is tall and the soil is soft. I can hear the voles moving under it. The wind moves the grass and makes a rustling sound. I like it. It is quiet. I can see the lights of the village from there, and the lights of the barn. I can hear the dogs barking. I can hear the cars. I can hear the people. I can hear the owls. I can

I fly over the meadow, past the stream, and up the hillside. The light fades, and the voles come out. I call, and the meadow answers. I swoop down, and the voles run. I catch them in the thicket, or on the bank, or in the ditch. I eat them, and I fly back to the oak. The light is gone, and the night is mine. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I do not know. The wood ends where the road begins, and beyond that, there is only darkness. I have never flown that far. The night is wide, and I do not need to see beyond the trees. I have my owlet, my nest, and the stream. That is enough.

My hunting ground is the meadow by the stream, the lane with the lights, and the woods beyond. I fly over the lane at night, and the lights are like fireflies. I hear the mice in the meadow, and the voles in the woods. The lane is dangerous, but I know where to fly low. The meadow is soft underfoot, and the stream is cold. I hunt there, and I sleep in the oak. Hoo... hoo-hoo

The grassy place is where the voles come out. It is the edge of the meadow, where the hedgerow meets the field. I sit on the fence post and watch. The grass is tall and green, and the voles run through it, sometimes under the fence, sometimes in the open. I hear them, and I strike. The grass is soft under my feet, and the air is cool. I do not like the grassy place. I like the oak.

I eat voles. Most of them. They are small, and they are under the leaves in the meadow. I hear them rustle, and I fly down and catch them with my feet. Sometimes I get a mouse or a shrew, but voles are the most common. They are the ones that keep me full through the long dark nights. I do not know what they are called, but I know their sound. My favourite prey is the vole. They are plentiful, and their scent is strong and easy to track. I can hear them moving under the leaves, and their squeaks are unmistakable. I strike fast and silent, and they don't see me coming. Sometimes I catch a shrew, but they're too small and not worth the effort. The voles fill my belly and keep me warm through the cold nights. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I do not hunt in the long grass. I hunt in the dark, in the wood, in the meadow, in the stream. The long grass is too thick, too tangled, and too full of the scent of the earth. I do not like it. I do not go there. I am an owl, and I belong to the trees.

I swallow whole the small things I catch, like voles, mice, and beetles. I can't chew them, so I just swallow them whole. It feels strange, but my stomach handles it. I also swallow whole the bits of fur and bones that come out of my crop. I don't like that part. It's messy. But I do it because I have to. I catch voles most. They are small, quick, and often under the leaves. I hear them rustling in the meadow and swoop down. Their squeaks are loud in the dark. I also catch shrews sometimes, but they are harder to find. The voles are the main ones.
A hollow in an old oak. The inside is dry and warm. I have a nest of moss and feathers. The entrance is a hole in the trunk. I can see the meadow from there. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is a hole in the trunk, wide enough for me to turn in, and deep enough to keep me warm. I have a nest of twigs and leaves inside, and I sleep there at night. The oak is on the edge of the meadow, where the wood meets the field. I can hear the stream from there, and the road that runs past the meadow. I am safe here, and I have been here for many

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is a hollow in the trunk, deep and dry, with a few branches sticking out. I can see the meadow from there, and the stream, and the lane with the lights. I am safe here, and the wind does not carry the scent of the lane. I have a mate, and we nest in the hollow. The hollow is my home.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is a hollow in the trunk, just above the roots, where the wind does not reach. I have been here for years, and the tree has grown around me. The hollow is dark, and I sleep in it when the night is still. I have a nest of twigs and leaves, and I keep it clean. I do not like the cold, but the hollow is warm. I have a mate, and we share the hollow

The hollow is in the old oak by the stream. It is wide enough for me to turn my head and see the whole tree. The bark is rough and the branches are thick. I have nested there for years. The wind comes through the leaves at night, and sometimes I hear the stream below. It is safe. I have raised my young there. The hollow is my home. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
